doc.title: Neal Caine interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, September 26, 2019

title: Who keeps the time: bassist or drummer
summary: Rowe opens with praise from Torkanowsky for Caine's Sinatra tribute bass playing, then asks who is responsible for time; Caine says the bass controls more than people realize.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: My name is Monk Rowe and I’m very pleased to have Neal Caine here, bassist and, you just got a big compliment from David Torkanowsky about a Frank Sinatra 100th birthday observance, a big band. And he said you really kicked some butt with your bass that night.
And the reason it came up was I asked him this question, I’m going to ask you too. In a jazz small group is it the bassist or the drummer who’s more responsible for the time?

Well you know ideally it should be everybody, but due to the importance of the bass and the drums it pretty much falls on us. Because horn players can kind of float around and nobody even really notices. I think it’s kind of both. I mean the drums obviously controls the percussion and stuff, but the bass is the nexus of rhythm and harmony. And honestly, I think the bass has a lot of control, more control than most people realize, over where the music goes, and it’s a lot more subtle. If I decide to go to a two beat or a four beat, or, I can control what happens. And also I’ve noticed over the years, I noticed that when I had a bad night the band kind of had a bad night. And if I had a good night, the whole band had a good night. Generally speaking.
